title: Manresa
hookLine: Ignatius spends months in a cave praying and writes notes that become the Spiritual Exercises

lines: A FEW DAYS BECOME A LONG STAY.
cards: A notebook, in the hand of a man dressed in sackcloth. On his way here he had stopped at the shrine of Our Lady at Montserrat, hung up his sword and dagger, and given his fine clothes to a beggar.
He meant to stay a few days in the small town down the hill. He stayed far longer, begging for food, letting his hair and nails grow, praying for hours every day.
Tradition points to a cave above the river where he went to pray. And all the while he kept writing in that notebook. The town is Manresa.

teach.b: Manresa was no peaceful retreat; his own account shows four sides of it. First, the dark. He was tormented by scruples, the fear that he hadn't confessed his sins fully.
He confessed again and again and found no rest. He says he was tempted to despair, and he doesn't hide it. Second, the school.

Later he described how God dealt with him there the way a schoolmaster deals with a child, one lesson at a time. He wasn't learning from books, but from what happened in him when he prayed. Third, the river.

One day, sitting by the river Cardoner, he says the eyes of his understanding began to open. He saw no vision, he says, but understood many things about faith and learning, and everything seemed new. Fourth, the notes.
Through it all, he wrote down what he noticed: what helped, what pulled him under, which way of praying led where.
Reworked over years, those notes became a small handbook called the Spiritual Exercises. It isn't a book to read straight through.
It's a set of instructions for someone guiding another person through prayer, step by step.
Some readers hear an echo of Mary in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Ignatius kept them on paper.
A soldier who knew nothing about prayer paid close attention, and wrote it down.

how: Catholics make the Spiritual Exercises on retreats, either as a silent retreat away from home or in daily life over a longer stretch, with a guide who meets them regularly.

games.q: you're Ignatius at Manresa. you've confessed your sins again and again, and the fear that you missed something won't leave. what do you do?
o: keep praying, and write down what helps and what drags you under.
games.why: he kept going and kept notes. what he learned about these struggles went into the Exercises, for others who would face the same.

practice: If you pray, pray a little while in whatever way you usually do; if you don't, just sit and let your mind be still. Then ask one plain question: what did I notice?
A word that stayed, a feeling that came or went, a person who came to mind; don't judge it, and if you like, put it into one line on paper.
